extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of constitutional law, political theory, and parliamentary practice
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of the functions, composition, and practical effects of the House of Commons and ministerial changes in a parliamentary constitution; normative claims about representation, teaching/informing functions, and ministerial responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliament should conform to public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: "Parliament conforms itself accurately enough, both as a chooser of executives and as a legislature, to the formed opinion of the country."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text argues Parliament ordinarily embodies the nation's formed opinion (both in policy and speech) and performs a 'lyrical' function of pouring out the nation's characteristic heart; this is presented as a central normative standard for evaluating the House of Commons, though qualified by exceptions (e.g., working-class exclusion, aristocratic influence). Examples and limits (foreign matters, errors of public opinion) are discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation must include advocates for special classes (informing function)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliament (or members of it) should "bring before the nation the ideas, grievances, and wishes of special classes"; this informing function is distinct from the teaching function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: special classes (e.g., artisans, trades) possess particular knowledge and grievances that Parliament must hear; admitting working-class representatives improves composition by ensuring those ideas are stated and examined. Historical practice (constituencies for shipping, wool, linen trades; members for Westminster) is cited as precedent and justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching (elevating) function should be concrete, popular, and short
rubrics_metrics.description: The teaching given in Parliament "must be popular, and to be popular it must be concrete, embodied, short"; the problem is "to know the highest truth which the people will bear, and to inculcate and preach that."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text criticises Parliament for performing poorly at elevating public opinion and stresses the Prime Minister's unique role as 'head-master' in imparting tone. It contrasts effective teaching (popular, concrete, succinct) with mere rhetoric or light tone (example: Palmerston's influence degrading the tone).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of working classes improves representational legitimacy (appearance matters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if theoretic proofs show adequacy, the absence of "notorious and palpable advocates" for large classes yields a diffused dissatisfaction because "gross appearances are great realities."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that visible absence of representatives (e.g., artisans) undermines public belief in the system; remedy is to give such classes members so the public sees that their grievances are represented. The 1832 single franchise is cited as having caused difficulty by removing sectional spokesmen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristocratic presence does not necessarily impair representation
rubrics_metrics.description: "Nor do I think the number of persons of aristocratic descent in Parliament impairs the accordance of Parliament with public opinion."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author contends aristocrats share the opinions of the landed gentry rather than forming a corporate caste; their presence can be desirable to match the 'dignified' and 'efficient' parts of institutions. The deferential instinct and electoral preferences are invoked to explain aristocratic election without implying distinct corporate interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliamentary debates should be instructive but are less able to elevate than written press
rubrics_metrics.description: While debates in English Parliament are "most instructive" (compared with American and French legislatures), the higher part of the press often has greater vigour and meaning than parliamentary speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparison: American Congress debates lack effect under presidential systems; French Chambers are often vain. The press's written discussions on great questions frequently convey more force and lasting meaning than spoken debates; this is a standard for evaluating parliamentary deliberation quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition balance: property + some 'mind' (no pure-mind representation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliament "represent[s] only mind coupled with property" and the author resists a representation of "pure mind" while admitting the country could "bear a little more mind."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'protected ability' critique (differential duty of wealth) is acknowledged but the author maintains that property shapes public opinion and must be present; still, excess opulent dulness in Parliament should be pruned slightly. This is a criterion for assessing desirable socio-economic composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ministry-wide changes create risk of inexperienced departmental heads
rubrics_metrics.description: Sudden wholesale changes of ministry "bring in on a sudden new persons and untried persons to preside over our policy" who lack subject familiarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Lord Cranborne (later Salisbury) as Indian Secretary lacking prior Indian experience; puzzle-analogy of matching offices; practical difficulty of finding twenty tried competent men at once. Use this to evaluate the cost of wholesale ministerial turnover.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequent ministry changes reduce ministers' interest and continuity in administration
rubrics_metrics.description: The system "keeps present ministers indifferent" because they may be removed by events beyond their control and thus lack motive to master their tasks fully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences include older, experienced ministers caring more about vicissitudes of office than their departmental work; young men still take interest but many do not. This is a normative metric when judging ministerial performance and incentives under parliamentary turnover.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rapid ministerial turnover risks harmful policy discontinuity
rubrics_metrics.description: "A sudden change of ministers may easily cause a mischievous change of policy"; continuity of mediocrity can be preferable to a 'hotch-potch' of excellences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by military/technical administration where steady selection and long experience yield balanced judgement; rapid succession prevents learning from predecessors and can produce desultory, incalculable policy shifts. Use to judge the strategic costs of frequent reshuffles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliamentary accountability (ministerial responsibility) is essential
rubrics_metrics.description: A minister "will have to give an account in Parliament of all branches of administration"; a predominant Parliament requires ministers to be accountable for all departments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author argues this feature is an inevitable and necessary aspect of parliamentary government because Parliament is an active corporate body that inquires into many subjects. This is used to defend ministerial selection from Parliament despite its costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanent clerks or outside administrators cannot effectively defend departments in Parliament
rubrics_metrics.description: When permanent officials (clerks) address Parliament they are "an outsider... speak under suspicion... put upon examination" and will often be ineffective or overwhelmed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: M. Guizot's experience and other argument: clerks are used to office routine, red tape, and cannot stand the hurly-burly of public assembly; they lose effect through interrogation and lack parliamentary votes. Thus departments need parliamentary members (ministers) to defend them rather than relying on permanent civil servants' speeches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Departments need authorised, competent parliamentary defenders (not merely 'benevolent amateurs')
rubrics_metrics.description: Without an authorised official defender the department is "helpless in Parliament" and vulnerable to opposition attack; volunteer defenders are often respectable but ineffectual and can be torn to shreds by parliamentary 'gladiators.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes the dynamics: opposition selects attack points, presses for documents, creates a public case of wrongdoing; weak defenders fail to withstand interrogation, leading to inquiries and loss of confidence. This is a practical criterion for evaluating departmental resilience before Parliament and the necessity of politically accountable defence.
